modelName: Levels of action · where the rules come from (added panel)
modelNote:
Not a figure in the lecture, which mentions the levels in one sentence: rules-in-use may be self-consciously changed in a collective-choice or constitutional-choice setting. Added here after Kiser and Ostrom (1982) and Ostrom (2005, chapter 2). Each level is itself an action situation. Its outcomes are the rules-in-use of the situation below. That makes the dashed 'changes the rules' feedback in Figure 2 visible. Everything in this panel is an addition, so it uses the dashed 'added' style throughout.

Lecture: Ostrom, E. (2010). Beyond Markets and States: Polycentric Governance of Complex Economic Systems. American Economic Review 100(3): 641–672 (the 2009 Nobel lecture).

Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5.5 · October 2026.

nodes.label: Levels of action · each level is an action situation whose outcomes are the rules below
METACONSTITUTIONAL
nodes.note:
Beneath (or above) all written rules: the shared sense of what a rule may be, who counts as a person with standing, what fairness means. Unwritten, which is why it is the strongest. The Institutional Grammar reaches it only as shared habits, recorded when seen.

Garden example: whether anyone thinks newcomers deserve a plot at all.

nodes.label: What people believe is even thinkable. Culture, identity, what counts as fair.

nodes.label: CONSTITUTIONAL
nodes.note:
The one-question test: does it change who may change the rules? The most leverage (Meadows 1 to 4).

Rule types here create the seats. Position rules make roles; boundary rules say who is a member; aggregation rules say how the rule-makers decide.

Garden example: who counts as a garden member, and how the spring meeting votes.

The health worker who is never at the table: there is no seat for them. Only a constitutional decision fixes it.

nodes.label: rules-in-use for the level below
nodes.note: The outcome of the situation above becomes a rule here. McGinnis calls such situations adjacent: outcomes in one determine a working part or a rule of the other.

nodes.label: COLLECTIVE CHOICE
nodes.note:
The one-question test: does it change a rule? (Meadows 5 and 6.) Design principle 3 lives here: the people affected help make and change the rules.

Garden example: the spring meeting amends the watering days.

A commons with operational rules and nothing above them can follow its rules but cannot change them.

nodes.label: OPERATIONAL
nodes.note:
The one-question test: does it change a number? The least leverage (Meadows 7 to 12), and where nearly all the effort goes.

Garden example: watering on your assigned day; the keeper suspends a gardener who breaks the rule.

A complaint that keeps recurring here is usually a rule problem one level up.

edges.label: seen and judged
edges.note: The feedback in Figure 2. People see outcomes, judge them, and take them to the level that can change the rule. Monitoring (principles 4A and 4B) and evaluative criteria feed this arrow.
